paragraphs.text: March 10. The martyrdom of Saint Quadratus and those with him. From many different cities, Christians had been seized in the time of the emperors Decius and Valerian and brought to the city of Nicomedia in Bithynia, and into prison

they had been thrown. They were kept under the strictest guard for questioning, so that, if they were willing to eat food offered in sacrifice, they would be released without torture, and each of them would return to his own homeland. There was great fear among the Christians in the city, especially because Emperor Decius was staying in Caesarea. Some fled into the mountains, while others hid in the countryside. But the tried and courageous servants of Christ remained in the city with hope and great joy, waiting in case they too might someday be found worthy to glorify God. One of them was the blessed Quadratus, distinguished by his stature, beauty, ancestry, wealth, and, what was truest of all, his devotion to God. He would come to the prison guard and the soldiers, giving them much gold, and freely serve the brothers imprisoned there, bringing each of them what he needed. He begged those more eager for martyrdom to remember him in the Lord’s kingdom, while he made the fearful courageous, urging them not to be afraid but to rejoice, reminding them that many people, departing this life neither easily nor with much suffering, were found worthy neither of this present life nor of rest there. And speaking of the healing of every affliction, he said that to suffer for Christ,

and still more to die for him, brings many great rewards. When the day came on which the proconsul sat in judgment before the people, he ordered the servants of Christ to be brought to the judgment seat. When they had been brought before him, the proconsul said to the servants of God, “Let each of you state his name, rank, and homeland.” But the blessed Quadratus, standing behind all the others, though held by no one, was the first of all to answer the proconsul’s question in a loud voice: “We are called Christians. This is our wonderful name. The glory and noble birth of us all are one and the same.” We are servants of Jesus Christ, the heavenly Lord and invisible God. The city of each of us is the heavenly Jerusalem, in which the Lord will settle all who place their hope in him. So now you have heard all about us, proconsul.” The proconsul, seeming beside himself at that man's boldness, said to his servants, “Bring that reckless man before me, so that I may see what his boldness has gained him.” When he heard this, he passed through the crowd and hurried forward himself. Standing before everyone and making the sign of the cross, he said to the proconsul, “I have come before you myself, proconsul, as the champion of my companions against your father the devil. Quickly, then, do what you wish, so that you may learn from

this trial that we are soldiers of Christ, and that by calling upon our Master, being invincible against the schemes of your warrior Satan, we stand firm in resistance.” The proconsul said, “Tell me your name first, reckless man, and your status.” Saint Quadratus said, “I told you that I am a Christian, as are all these whom you see, my brothers. As for status, I have none, but we are servants of the Lord. This is our noble birth.” The proconsul said, “You ought not to call yourself a Christian, since the decree of the invincible emperors condemns you to death. I see that you are handsome and very eloquent. So listen to me, my friend, and I will report about you to the emperor and intercede for you to receive a high office, if only you show gratitude to the gods.” The most blessed martyr of Christ, Quadratus, said, “Proconsul, do not speak foolishly of gods. For there are not many gods, but one God, the Father, from whom all things come, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things exist.” The proconsul said, “There are indeed many gods. The emperor has commanded sacrifices to twelve gods, whom we ought to obey and worship.” Saint Quadratus boldly cried out in a loud voice, saying, “It is not good to have many gods. Let there be one God, one emperor!” Then the proconsul became angry and ordered him stripped, stretched out on a board, and beaten with rawhide lashes,

saying, “Tell me your name.” But when he did not answer, the proconsul asked the servants, “What is his name?” They said, “Quadratus. He is also of noble birth.” The proconsul said, “Spare him, and lift him off the wooden frame.” And he said to him, “What is this you have done to us?” “Why did you cast off your rank?” And calling him close to him, he said to him, “Why have you abandoned your rank and lineage and embraced the vain Christian faith?” But blessed Quadratus said, “I have chosen rather to lie at the threshold of my God's house than to live in the dwellings of sinners.” The proconsul said, “Listen to me and sacrifice to the gods, so that you do not die a miserable death like a criminal.” Saint Quadratus said, “Blessed is the man who does not walk in the way of the ungodly and has not sat in the seat of the destructive, but his delight shall be in the law of the Lord.” [?] The proconsul said, “Do not deceive yourself, Quadratus. For every Christian is subject to the emperor's punishment, whether poor or rich, whether a dignitary or a peasant. The judgment will spare none of them.” The saint said, “Yes, for God's Scripture says: ‘There is neither slave nor free, neither rich nor poor, neither barbarian nor Scythian, neither Greek nor Jew. For we are all one in the Lord.’ Therefore I beg you: the punishment of the emperor and the nobles—carry it out against me without delay, for I am

a Christian. My lineage and dignity are with the saints who possess splendor, and not from people who exist today but will not exist tomorrow.” The proconsul said, “Listen to me and sacrifice, and enjoy your fill of this life and this world.” And as he said this, the proconsul burst into tears with loud groaning. But the valiant martyr Quadratus said to him, “Do not offer me a serpent's schemes, and do not shed the devil's tears, you dog and plunderer! For you will not deceive me, God's servant.” Maximus the magistrate said, “You crafty man! My illustrious lord has pity on you, but you insult him.” Saint Quadratus said, “Let him weep for himself, for there is no need to weep for me or pity me. If the proconsul is the judge, then who are you to speak before him? This is enough for us. But if you too want to be in charge, may God curse you!” The court recorder said, “By your good fortune, my lord proconsul, if you let this man go like this, he will not hesitate to revile even the emperors themselves, and you will bring no small trouble upon us.” Saint Quadratus said, “Truly, as God's Scripture says, ‘Why did the nations grow arrogant?’” And the peoples plotted vain things. The kings of the earth took their stand, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ. For even now, from vain

rulers, the servant of God receives judgment. The proconsul said, “Strip the ungrateful man and beat him again, so that he may come to his senses and obey the gods and the commands of our lords the emperors.” As he was being beaten, the blessed man said, “Glory to you, God, Lord Jesus Christ, because you have deemed even me, sinful and unworthy, worthy to suffer all this for your name, so that I too, wretched as I am, may be counted among your servants whom you love. I thank you, Lord. Master, grant that I may be filled with your Holy Spirit. Grant me wisdom concerning you, and preserve my faith unshaken. Make me wise with your wisdom, for now is the time for your protection. Now is the time for your favor; now is the time for your help. Enlighten me and strengthen me with your promise. Receive me, so that your name may be glorified through me, your wretched servant. Bring me to perfection in your name, and bring me to your Father. Acknowledge before him that I am your servant. Yes, Lord Jesus Christ, I beg you, bring my race to its end.” When those beating him had changed shifts five times and had grown exhausted, blood flowed in streams, together with pieces of flesh, from the blessed martyr. The proconsul said to the saint, “Do you at least now believe in the gods, Quadratus?” Blessed Quadratus

said, “The idols of the pagans are silver and gold. They have mouths but do not speak. They have eyes but do not see. They have ears but do not hear. They have nostrils but do not smell. They have hands but do not feel. They make no sound with their throats. Those who make them will become like them, as will all who trust in them.” Perennis the proconsul said, “You blaspheme in obscure language, thinking to find fault. Listen, then, Quadratus, and sacrifice to the gods.” Saint Quadratus said, “You were right to say ‘in obscure language,’ for the truth seems obscure to you, while falsehood seems clear. So, in plain language, I will begin with ancestral expressions. Let it be known to you that I will not sacrifice to your gods.” And I will not obey the commands of Caesar or the governor. If you wish to torture me, then do as you will, and send me more quickly to the heavenly King.” The proconsul said, “By the gods, I will not spare you, but will destroy you with various tortures and a bitter death, you wretch.” When day had already come, he ordered them all to be taken to prison. He ordered crushed potsherds to be scattered beneath the blessed martyr’s back and a large stone to be placed on his chest, and his feet to be put in [?], and his whole body to be bound in irons. And they did this

to the saint and left him neglected like this for many days. But blessed Quadratus, as a truly valiant sufferer for the true faith, bravely endured those cruel tortures and did not turn away from his hope in God. The proconsul went to the city of Nicaea and ordered the holy martyrs to follow. He entered the temple, sacrificed to the idols, and ordered the saints to be brought before him. Saint Quadratus also entered, like a valiant warrior trusting in his own strength as he goes to meet his enemies, advancing proudly at the front against them. He looks ahead, displaying the cross on his face, and terrifies the enemy ranks. So too this valiant man walked before all the saints, showing a face radiant and strong; and the chains that lay upon him he wore like a precious ornament, exulting and rejoicing, so that the Greek philosophers marveled at Christian wisdom and endurance, and glorified God, saying, “Truly great is the Christian faith!” And many of them came to believe in God. When they stood before the proconsul, Saint Quadratus begged the attendants to bring him in first. When he had been brought before the proconsul, the proconsul said to the saint, “Sacrifice to the gods.”

Saint Quadratus said, “I am a servant of Christ, who said, ‘Let the gods who did not make heaven and earth perish.’” The proconsul said, “Sacrifice, Quadratus.” The martyr said, “I will not sacrifice. I have already told you that I am Christ’s servant.” The proconsul said, “You must obey the emperors’ laws, not this Christ of yours, as you say.” Saint Quadratus said, “I obey my King, Christ, and not men who do not know God. We have been commanded to pray for them, so that perhaps they may turn and come to the knowledge of the truth, but never to sacrifice to idols.” The proconsul said, “Then if you pray for the emperors, you must also obey their commands. For it is written, ‘Render to Caesar what is Caesar’s.’ and to God what belongs to God. Saint Quadratus said, “I have paid my debt to Caesar for my estate. And I must also discharge the debt I owe my God. He has ordered Christians to offer sacrifices or else die if they refuse to sacrifice. But we are ready to die for confessing Christ, not just once, but thousands of times.” The proconsul said, “Do you see how many Christians have sacrificed to the gods? Do you think you are better than they are?” Saint Quadratus said, “I am far better and more nobly born, because I have not sacrificed. Where are those who have sacrificed?

I do not see them.” And the proconsul ordered them to be brought before him. As they were about to bring them in, blessed Quadratus, so that they would not see him simply standing there, said to the proconsul, “Order them to untie me.” When he had been untied, the blessed man ran into the temple, smashed all the idols, and threw them to the ground. When the priests saw what had happened, they seized him and, together with the soldiers, brought him before the proconsul. The proconsul became angry and ordered them to hang him up and scrape his flesh. When the saint had been hung up, he began to glorify God. Blessed Quadratus said to them, “O wretched men, utterly wretched! What have you suffered, that you lost heart so quickly, denied Christ the Master, and handed yourselves over to the devil? Did you not believe that there would be a resurrection of the dead? Do you not know that there will be an unquenchable fire, and a worm that never sleeps, and bottomless mire, and the deepest pit? What answer will you give on the great and glorious day of the coming of our Savior Jesus Christ? Open the eyes of your mind and see from where you have fallen, and where you have landed. You have abandoned the kingdom of heaven and become soldiers of the worthless slave who, when his master has gone away, beats and kills his fellow servants. His master will come and cut him in two. Understand what you have done: fearing short-lived

torments, you have handed yourselves over to eternal torment. You will see what awaits you from the righteous judge, Jesus Christ, who will repay each person according to their deeds.” As blessed Quadratus was saying this, those who had denied their faith cried out loudly with tears and said, “Lord, we were afraid of the torments and were swept away like irrational animals. Like lambs among wolves, we were seized and scattered, for our own sins have ensnared us.” And wishing to live in this short-lived life, we have died in the age to come. So what shall we do? We do not know, wretched as we are.” But blessed Quadratus was filled with joy at their repentance. And seeing their tears, he said to them, “Have hope, brothers, for our Lord Jesus Christ is merciful. Fall down before him with tears. Stand firm even now in your confession of the Savior. Cleanse yourselves of sins with your own blood, and where you were defeated in the flesh, overcome through strength of soul.” Then, when they had cried out loudly for a long time and had thrown themselves to the ground and sprinkled their heads with dust, such trembling came upon those standing nearby that it was not only the Christians who wept with them. For those living in the city of Nicaea, alarmed by the shouting and wailing, gathered at that place, men and women

and children, Jews and Greeks, and a multitude of Christians who had been keeping themselves hidden, so that there was no room for the crowd. Angered by this, the proconsul ordered blessed Quadratus to be scraped still more and his sides to be burned with flaming torches. Beside himself with rage, he fell from his seat, inhumanly ordering tortures to be inflicted on him. But Quadratus, Christ’s valiant champion, as though he felt none of the tortures, instructed those who were repenting, saying, “Pray earnestly to the Lord, brothers; that is good.” But they said, “We are not worthy to utter the holy name of Christ.” Rebuking them, he said to them, “Pray to God, brothers, pray. Come close to me.” And when they came forward and fell down before him, weeping bitterly, and everyone there was weeping with them, blessed Quadratus raised his voice and cried out with tears, saying, “Blessed God, who sent your only-begotten Son Jesus Christ and through him reconciled yourself to us, and, while we were enemies, made us your own through your surpassing love for humankind; who made all creation for the sake of humankind, made in your image, so that they might be nourished by the creatures you made: now, Master, drive Satan away from these servants of yours. Accept now, Master, these kinsmen

of mine, who became entangled in the devil’s snares but now flee to your goodness and love for humankind. Do not, then, be angry with them because they denied you. wood. Yet they stand unbending. Accept the gift of me, your unworthy servant. And make them worthy to join your heavenly and true soldiers. You yourself work [?] a sign for good, so that they may know that you have shown them mercy. And do not reject them as they repent. Yes, Master, Lord Jesus Christ, hear me, your servant. And accept my soul in exchange for their souls, for glory belongs to you forever. Amen. And when all the brethren had said “Amen” in a loud voice, the candles suddenly went out. And the hands of the servants who were torturing them grew powerless, and a bright cloud came over all the saints. But darkness and gloom poured down upon the proconsul and the pagans, so that the proconsul lost his senses from fear and trembled together with his advisers, as they thought that even the city was about to collapse. When a deep silence had fallen, an angelic voice was heard singing and glorifying God. When two hours had passed, the darkness gradually began to disperse. And the pagans began to look at the saints and to see the light surrounding them. For those who had repented began to cry out in a loud voice and say, “We have sinned and acted lawlessly.

Forgive us, Savior!” The proconsul, barely having come to his senses, ordered them to be taken to prison and securely confined. And they took the blessed Quadratus down from the wooden frame and threw him into prison and secured him. The next morning, the proconsul took his seat on the judgment seat and ordered those who had repented to be brought before him. After questioning them and discovering their earnest and unwavering confession of faith, and being unable to change their minds, he ordered each of them to be taken to his own country and city and burned alive there. But he ordered the blessed Quadratus, together with the others, to go on to the Hellespont. All the saints went away filled with joy and glorifying God. And so each of them was taken to his own country, and they died in Christ. The proconsul went to the city of Apamea and, after sacrificing to the idols, ordered the holy martyrs to be brought before him. And he said to the blessed Quadratus, “Will you sacrifice to the gods, then, you sorcerer and wicked man, or not?” But the valiant martyr Quadratus said, “Call your father that, since that is what he is. For I am a Christian, and I know neither sorcery nor trickery.” “And I do not sacrifice to demons.” Seeing that the saint’s whole body had been flayed, the proconsul said to his companions, “I do not know what tortures to inflict on this man doomed to a miserable death.” But they did not know and gave no answer,

for they could see that his body could no longer endure torture. The proconsul ordered them to bring a sack, put him into it, and dig a pit, and to suspend him in the pit in the sack and beat him with clubs. After a long time had passed, he ordered them to take him out of the sack, thinking that he was dead. When they untied the sack, the saint sprang out and stood upright. The proconsul said, “He has not [?] yet felt the tortures.” Saint Quadratus looked up to heaven and said, “I thank you, Lord Jesus Christ, for their blows became like children’s arrows, and their strength failed within them. But you gave me strength and made me strong.” And he said to the proconsul, “You wretched man, do you see, and do you still put me to the test? Whatever you can do, do it—only do it quickly.” The proconsul flew into a rage and said to him, “After all this toil, I will destroy you, even if you put your trust in your sorcery.” Saint Quadratus cried out, “Blessed are you, Lord our God, for you have delivered our life from the hand of death. Now, therefore, I will give glory to you, our Most High God.” The proconsul ordered him to be taken ahead to Caesarea. After entering the city, the proconsul sacrificed to demons the following morning and ordered blessed Quadratus to be brought before him. He asked him whether he was willing to sacrifice. But when he learned that the blessed martyr remained steadfast,

he said to him, “The tortures you have suffered are enough for you. Come forward and sacrifice to the gods.” But blessed Quadratus said, “You have been playing with me with these tortures of yours.” The proconsul became angry and ordered them to stretch him out on sharp stones and beat him all over his body with ox sinews. As he was being beaten, the blessed man glorified God, saying, “Many times they fought against me, yet they did not overcome me. Sinners hammered upon my back; they prolonged their lawlessness.” When he finished the psalm, the proconsul said, “Keep beating him without stopping.” But the valiant martyr Quadratus said, “Beat me, beat me! It is the flesh that you are harming.” but you will not harm the soul. The proconsul said, “You wretch, you have surpassed an evil demon.” Saint Quadratus said, “By my Lord Jesus Christ, a very evil one indeed—and not just one, but I have become master of his whole army, for the sake of my Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever. Amen.” When the multitude of the brethren answered, “Amen,” the proconsul became very angry and ordered two men to be seized from the crowd and brought to him. When the two had been seized, he left Saint Quadratus and began to interrogate the blessed Saturninus and Rufinus, for these were their names. He had them hung up and ordered them to be torn with iron claws

until their entrails were about to spill out onto the ground. While being tortured, the two blessed men begged Saint Quadratus and all the brethren standing there to pray to God for them. Saint Quadratus cried out and said, “Lord Jesus Christ, [?] of the invisible Father, send your help upon them and protect them. Yes, God of the humble, have mercy on your servants and give them endurance and victory to the very end.” When a long time had passed, and the two gave no answer—for because of their many tortures they could not even speak— the proconsul ordered them to be taken down and handed over to the executioners, who were to behead them as they traveled along the road to the Hellespont. When the two had thus met their end, men who loved God and Christ followed them along the road and took their precious relics, giving the executioners much gold. They brought them to their own cities and laid them to rest with honor. The proconsul ordered the blessed Quadratus, together with the others, to follow him to Apollonia. The impious proconsul entered the temple of Apollo and ordered Saint Quadratus to be brought in, along with the others. When they had been brought in, he tried to force them to sacrifice to the impious demons. He said to the blessed Quadratus,

“Listen to me, then, and give up your madness. Why do you disgrace your rank and your family? Acknowledge the gods and save yourself, and I will order the physicians to heal you. Only sacrifice to the gods. Approach Asclepius, and he will heal you. Fear the majesty of the gods and the great and valiant Apollo, and Heracles, who is king of all, and Zeus, the thrice-great, Ares, and Poseidon. Have you never sailed upon the sea, then, so that you might know the fear he inspires? Or else bow down to the sun, which shines throughout the whole world. Has he too died, as you blasphemously claim? Is he not in heaven?” But blessed Quadratus said, “I worship the true God and his only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ, and I do not deny the Holy Spirit. Rather, I tremble before his might, and I continually praise and glorify his indescribable power. I do not bow down to dead idols. I do not fear demons, nor you, whose authority lasts only a short time. In just a few more days I will go to my Lord, but you will weep bitterly because you refused to acknowledge the true God, who gave you life, you son of Satan, companion of unclean demons, rabid dog, blood-drinking serpent, flesh-devouring sword, ferocious beast! Are you not ashamed to sacrifice to stones before the people, before such a great multitude

of people—stones that receive nothing? Cooks, who are servants of human beings, are purer than you, because they slaughter cleanly in courtyards for people to eat, and not for demons. But you sacrifice to senseless idols before the people and feel no shame, for although you slaughter for a stone, you yourselves eat. Let the one who receives the sacrifice come, you shameless people! Let him appear; let him ask for himself. Let him receive it and eat it. Let your stone god say what he wants slaughtered for him: a goat, an ox, or a bird—whichever he values more. Be ashamed, you shameful children! For although you are demon-possessed, you think that we, who are of sound mind, are mad.” And as he was saying this, the proconsul became angry and ordered them to mix salt with vinegar, pour it over his wounds, and rub them with cloth. When the saint fell silent, the impious Perennius ordered them to heat irons until they were very hot and burn his sides with them. But blessed Quadratus patiently endured the pain and prayed silently in his mind. His lips moved, but his voice could not be heard. When the servants grew exhausted, he ordered them to take him down and lead him into prison. The next morning the proconsul ordered the saint to be led ahead to the Hellespontine

island. When the proconsul had crossed the River Rhyndacus, the ruler of that place came out to meet him, along with the people who had gathered from the temples, but who in truth longed to see Christ’s suffering martyr. For the report of his martyrdom had already spread throughout all Asia and even throughout the whole world. The proconsul ordered everyone to go ahead to the village lying farther on, called Serucomin [?]. For many pagan temples had been built there. After staying there, he took his seat the next morning. He ordered the holy martyr Quadratus to be brought before him. All the people gathered and stood watching the blessed martyr Quadratus. Although his whole body was covered in blood and swollen like an inflated wineskin, his face appeared calm and radiant. He smiled as the attendants led him. For because of the many tortures they had inflicted on him, he could no longer even walk. He had been carried in a cart the whole way. When he stood before the proconsul, the proconsul said to him, “Have you come to your senses, then, Quadratus, or not?” He cried out in a very loud voice and said, “From my earliest childhood I have lived chastely. From my mother’s womb I have been a Christian, and I know no other God except my Lord Jesus Christ.” Then the proconsul became angry and ordered

a fire to be kindled and a griddle to be placed over it. The attendants kindled the fire, and the griddle grew so hot that it looked like fire. The proconsul ordered the holy man to be placed on the griddle. But blessed Quadratus said, “I will climb onto the griddle myself, and I will not delay.” Making the sign of Christ, he lay down on the griddle. The devil’s servants threw onto the griddle pitch, oil, and reeds. But holy Quadratus sang, “O God, attend to my help; O Lord, hurry to help me. Let those who seek my life be ashamed and disgraced. Let those who wish me harm turn back and be put to shame.” When he had finished the psalm, about two hours having passed, the holy man began to mock the proconsul, saying, “This fire of yours is cold, and the iron of the griddle is softer than your heart. You have done well, then. I am weary from the journey. You ordered me to rest on this soft bed. Now I have rested and regained my strength.” As he said this, the holy martyr turned over on the griddle as though it were a properly made bed. After a long time had passed and the fire had not harmed him at all, the proconsul ordered them to take him off the griddle, lead him up a hill a little outside the village, and with a sword

to cut off his head. Having received the sentence, and hastening toward the kingdom of heaven, the blessed Quadratus sang, saying, “Blessed is the Lord, who will not give us over as prey to their teeth.” And some of the brothers who were following him sang with him all the way to the place where he was to meet his end. He finished the psalm, and after praying at length and giving thanks to God, bending his knees and stretching out his neck, in his good confession of faith, he was beheaded, to the glory and praise of Christ our God, now and always and forever and ever.
